To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
farmers generally did not follow nutrient management plans and did not apply N at rates recommended by universities or fertilizer dealers.
farmers do not fully adopt recommended nutrient management practices and that farmers need to be convinced that nutrient management will improve their farm operations.

(i) farmers generally do not use nutrient management plans or soil test recommendations, (ii) farmers do not trust N recommendations, and (iii) watershed education, technical assistance, and funding resources can improve nutrient management.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the adoption of nutrient management by farmers.
the adoption of nutrient management plans by farmers, the barriers to adoption, and the strategies that have been effective in promoting adoption.
understanding why farmers use, or do not use, nutrient management.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of nutrient management plans is not widespread and that farmers are not fully adopting nutrient management recommendations.
farmers are not using nutrient management plans to reduce nutrient losses to water resources.
the use of nutrient management plans by farmers is not widespread.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the adoption of nutrient management by farmers is not a straightforward, linear process.
farmers are not adopting nutrient management because they are not being asked to adopt it.
the most effective nutrient management programs are those that focus on a limited number of farms and that are willing to make investments to reduce the risk of farmers adopting nutrient management.
The main takeaway from our work is that

nutrient management plans are not enough to ensure nutrient reductions in impaired watersheds; they must be accompanied by meaningful investment and a focus on farmer adoption of nutrient management practices.
farmers will not adopt nutrient management plans unless they are provided with meaningful incentives and support.
nutrient management is not a simple, one-time, decision.
